Metadata.title: AgiMate — agents with scoped access
Metadata.description: Every agent has its own skills, its own connectors, its own access, and you can add as many as you need: one per task, or a team working a shared board. Agents never see the keys to your services, reach only the connectors you opened for them, and every call goes through a rule and into the log.
Metadata.ogDescription: A harness around any language model: tools, connectors to your systems, rules checked before the call, and a log of every action. Every agent has its own access.

hero.title: Your agents
hero.tagline:
A library of ready-to-use AI agents.
Create a new agent in three steps.
In the cloud, with fine-grained access control.

harness.title: What a harness is
harness.subtitle: On its own, a model only writes text. To send an email or file a task it needs tools, keys to your services, rules and a log. We call all of that the harness. It is shared by every agent and configured for each one separately.

items.title: Tools
items.tech: Tools come from connections: an MCP server, your own API behind a key, Telegram, your phone or computer. An agent sees a tool only while that connection is bound to it. For example, sending a Telegram message or reading a spreadsheet row.

items.title: Skills
items.tech: A skill says in what order to call tools, what not to do, and which connections it needs. One skill can go on several agents; ready-made ones are in the catalogue.
items.plain: A skill gives the agent the steps: read the receipt, add the expense to the sheet, and ask you if the totals don't match.

items.title: Keys stay on the platform
items.tech: Connection keys and tokens are stored on the platform. The model sees only tool names and descriptions, and the key is added after it has chosen a call. The exception is the LLM provider key: the model can't be reached without it, so it goes to the platform worker.

items.title: Rules before the call
items.tech: You can allow or deny an individual tool, limit its parameters, or close a connection entirely.
items.plain: The agent may read your mail but not delete it. The check runs before the request reaches the mail server.

items.title: Action log
items.tech: For every run you can see the agent's steps, each call with its parameters and the service's answer, and how many tokens each model used.

items.title: Where the agent runs
items.tech: The agent runs on the platform: in our cloud, or on your own server if you host AgiMate yourself. Your phone and computer connect as connectors and carry out commands, but the agent itself never runs on them.
items.plain: So every call passes through the platform, where the rules get a chance to work. An agent running directly on your machine talks to the system with nothing in between to check it.

agents.title: An agent's specialisation rests on its access
agents.subtitle: A model can break an instruction if it's pushed hard enough. A tool from a connection that isn't bound to the agent can't be called at all: for that agent it doesn't exist. So an agent's role is set first of all by what it is connected to.

axes.title: Its own model
axes.tech: The provider and a priority list of models are set per agent: for chat, for reading images and for generating them. An analyst can get a strong model, while a reminder agent does fine on a cheap one.

axes.title: Its own instructions
axes.tech: Each agent has its own instruction text, from a ready-made role or written from scratch. One answers customers briefly; another goes through a report and cites the numbers.

axes.title: Its own access
axes.tech: Connections are bound to a specific agent, and inside a binding there are rules for individual tools and their parameters.
axes.plain: Like staff passes: the accountant gets the spreadsheets, the secretary gets mail and the calendar.

axes.title: Its own skills
axes.tech: Skills are added to a specific agent, and tools that other agents' skills need don't appear on it. The less an agent has lying around, the less often it reaches for the wrong tool.

howItWorks.lede: Every call goes through a rule
howItWorks.intro: A trigger, say a new email, arrives from a connection or a device. The platform checks it against the rules and hands it to one agent. When the agent needs to act, it calls a tool through the core, and that call is checked the same way. The core adds the keys; the agent never gets them. Allowed and denied events are written to the trigger log and the tool call log.
howItWorks.sr: Diagram: triggers from connections and devices (Mail, Calendar, Laptop, Android) pass a policy check in the core and go to one agent. Tool calls pass the same check, and the agent's answer goes to the user in the web chat, Telegram, the phone app or an IDE. Below the diagram are two logs, triggers and tool calls, with each row marked allowed or denied. Packets on the diagram carry Greek letters, which match them to rows in the log.

connector.title: Connector
connector.body: An external service: mail, calendar, messenger, MCP server. Its credentials are stored here, in the platform.

device.title: Device
device.body: A companion on your own machine or phone. It raises triggers of its own, such as a watched file or a geofence, and exposes only the tools built into it.

rules.title: Policy
rules.body: Checked before the service is called.

channel.title: User Channel
channel.body: The one way out to a person. The agent's answer leaves through this channel into whichever messenger the conversation is in.

useCases.title: What you can build today
useCases.subtitle: Each scenario is built from parts the dashboard already has. Under the description you can see which ones.

items.title: An agent in Telegram
items.description: Connect Telegram as a channel and the agent starts answering there according to your instructions. You can read the conversations in the dashboard afterwards.

items.title: A scheduled check
items.description: On a schedule, the agent checks an external service and sends you the result. For example, it checks every hour whether your site is up, or collects new leads each morning. A job can be paused or run outside the schedule.

items.title: Reacting to an event
items.description: An external system sends a webhook, say about a new payment or a failed build, and the agent decides what to do next. Deliveries and tool calls are visible in the trigger log.

items.title: An agent on your device
items.description: The Android and desktop apps connect your device to the agent. A notification arrives, the phone rings or a file changes, and the agent receives it as an event. In reply it can send a push, read text aloud or run a command on the device.

items.title: An agent in your IDE
items.description: Over the ACP protocol the agent connects to your code editor. It keeps the same skills, access rules and log as in Telegram or the web chat.

items.title: Your own service as a tool
items.description: Connect your API as an app with a key or as an MCP server, and its methods become the agent's tools. Rules decide which of them the agent may call.

items.title: A team of agents on a shared board
items.description: Several agents work from one task board: each task has a status, an assignee and a comment thread. Changes on the board show up in the dashboard immediately.

security.title: Scoped access is built into the architecture

items.title: The agent only sees what's bound
items.description: Until a connection is bound to an agent, its tools don't exist for that agent. Bindings are visible from both sides: on the agent and on the connection.

items.title: Rules are checked before the call
items.description: You can deny an agent a single tool, limit the values of its parameters or close a connection entirely. If a rule blocks the call, the request never reaches the external service, and the denial is written to the log.

items.title: Every action logged
items.description: The log shows which agent called a tool, with what parameters, and what the service answered. Errors and policy denials can be filtered out on their own.

models.title: Your model, your key
models.subtitle: Tokens are billed by your provider at your rate

items.title: Your key at your provider
items.description: Connect a provider with your own key, and tokens are billed by that provider at your rate. The platform takes the model list from the provider and marks the ones that are currently unavailable.

items.title: Different models for different jobs
items.description: Chat, image recognition and image generation each get their own priority list of models. If the first model on the list is unavailable, the platform uses the next one.

items.title: Spend visible in the dashboard
items.description: The dashboard shows how many tokens each agent spent and on which model. If you don't have a key yet, you can start on the platform's free allowance.

meta.title: Privacy Policy — AgiMate
meta.description: What data AgiMate stores, where keys and logs live. The document is in progress — the substance is set out here.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.draftNotice: The final wording will land before public launch. While the document is being prepared, here is how things work today.

sections.title: What we store
sections.body: Your OAuth provider profile (name and email address), the agents you create, skills, connections, and your conversations with agents.

sections.title: Tokens and keys
sections.body: The refresh token lives in an HTTP-only cookie and is unreachable from JavaScript. LLM provider keys and connection secrets are stored server-side and are never shown again in the interface.

sections.title: Third-party services
sections.body: Model requests go to the provider whose key you connected. Tool calls go to the services you connected yourself.

sections.title: Logs
sections.body: We keep a log of tool calls and triggers — it exists for your own troubleshooting and is visible in the dashboard.

sections.title: Self-hosted
sections.body: When deployed on your own server, data never leaves your infrastructure.

sections.title: Deletion
sections.body: Write to us and we'll delete your account and the data attached to it.

Privacy.contactBody: Write to us in the community chat and we'll answer.

hero.title: An agent platform

hero.note: Terms depend on the scenario — we agree them case by case.

audience.title: Who it's for
audience.subtitle: Three situations where an agent platform is cheaper to take than to build.

items.title: Inference providers, clouds and hosting
items.have: Models, compute and tokens you already bill for, and a customer base of your own.
items.missing: A product to spend it in. A bare API only sells itself to developers.
items.gain: The customer comes for the agents and stays for the inference. The split between a platform pool and the customer's own key is already in the product, and so is per-user spend.

items.title: Integrators and automation studios
items.have: A flow of clients, the expertise, and scenarios assembled by hand.
items.missing: Every project starts from scratch, and keeping a zoo of bots alive eats the margin.
items.gain: One platform under your brand, with a separate perimeter per client. Instead of building from scratch — configuring agents, connectors and access rules.

items.title: SaaS vendors
items.have: A product, subscribers, and data worth pointing an agent at.
items.missing: The agent layer inside it. Writing one yourself means running a second product instead of your own.
items.gain: Agents inside your product rather than a second dashboard next to it. Connectors, app keys and channels come ready.

whiteLabel.title: What white label means here
whiteLabel.subtitle: The core stays shared and keeps updating; the storefront is yours.

items.title: Your economics
items.description: A shared pool with a free allowance, the customer's own key, or both. Token spend is counted per user — there is something to put into your billing.

items.title: Your perimeter
items.description: Self-hosted: data, keys and logs stay on your side. Not a single call goes through us.

steps.title: Download the APK
steps.description: Download the latest APK version from GitHub Releases.

steps.title: Allow installation from unknown sources
steps.description: Settings → Security → Unknown sources (or allow for your browser).

steps.title: Install and open the app
steps.description: Run the APK file, wait for installation, and open AgiMate.

steps.title: Enter the device key
steps.description: Create a key in Dashboard → Mobile Devices and paste it in the app settings.

steps.title: Enable the triggers you need
steps.description: Select triggers and grant the required permissions.
